strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior work on dense associative memory (Krotov-Hopfield model) has focused almost exclusively on equilibrium/storage-capacity properties, and this paper is (to the authors' knowledge) the first to attempt a dynamical analysis via generating functional analysis (GFA).

The technical machinery (GFA, saddle-point analysis, effective single-site process) is applied carefully and the derivation of the noise term (Lemma 1) and the resulting saddle-point equations (Proposition 1) appear methodologically sound and consistent with the classical GFA literature for spin-glass/Hopfield dynamics.

The paper draws a useful connection between Krotov's dense associative memory and the closely related n-body Hopfield model of Gardner and Abbott, showing where the two models agree and differ (self-coupling terms, detailed balance) and recovering known equilibrium results as a special/limiting case.

Concrete, interpretable output is produced: approximate recursion for the overlap, storage capacity estimates for several values of n, and attraction-basin curves, giving some quantitative insight into how these models are expected to behave dynamically.
weaknesses: The central quantitative results (storage capacity values, attraction basin curves in Fig. 1, Corollary 1) are derived from an approximation that neglects the retarded self-interaction term (Γ=0), which the paper itself identifies as the key complicating dynamical feature; the 'exact' GFA solution (Proposition 1) is never actually solved or evaluated, so the paper's advertised exact dynamical analysis is largely not realized in the reported results.

There is no numerical simulation of the actual finite-N network to validate either the exact GFA equations or the approximate dynamics/attraction-basin predictions; for a paper whose main claim is a novel dynamical/GFA analysis, the absence of any Monte Carlo or direct simulation check on convergence, capacity, or basin size is a significant gap in rigor.

The relevance to a general AI audience is thin: the paper motivates itself via Transformer-inspired modern Hopfield networks and the Hopfield layer, but the actual analysis is restricted to the classical binary-pattern, power-function F(x)=x^n Krotov model (n≥3, discrete states), not the continuous-state/exponential-energy Hopfield layers that are of most current interest to the ML community; the practical implications for modern architectures are not developed.

Several claims are asserted without full justification in the main text (e.g., 'it turns out that the system can be described in terms of the three quantities...', Lemma 1's derivation is only sketched, the Maxwell-construction consistency claim in Section 4.3/4.4 is stated but not derived), and no appendix/supplementary proofs appear to be referenced, limiting reproducibility and verifiability.

The manuscript has numerous typographical, grammatical, and formatting issues (e.g., 'Preliminalies' section header, garbled reference [13] title, inconsistent notation such as reused symbols Q and K in Eq. 16, awkward phrasing throughout), which detracts from clarity and suggests the paper is not fully polished for submission.

The novelty of the technique itself is incremental: GFA for parallel-dynamics Ising-like networks is a well-established tool (Gardner-Derrida-Mottishaw, Crisanti-Sompolinsky, Rieger et al., cited as [10-13]); the contribution is largely in applying existing machinery to a new but structurally similar model rather than developing new theoretical tools, which limits the paper's broader significance for a top-tier AI venue.

The paper does not discuss finite-size effects, does not compare against any baseline dynamical theories (e.g., statistical neurodynamics / Amari-Maginu style approaches, cited but not used comparatively), and does not explore how tight the O(N^-1) approximation error terms are, leaving the practical accuracy of the theory unquantified.

strengths: First asymptotically exact dynamical analysis of dense associative memory using generating functional analysis (GFA), filling a genuine gap since only equilibrium/storage-capacity properties had previously been studied for this model.

Technically rigorous derivation: the paper carefully tracks combinatorial factors (via the A(ℓ,k) counting arguments) needed to correctly average over non-recalled patterns, and provides detailed proof sketches in the appendices for both the generating functional (Lemma 1) and the saddle-point equations (Proposition 1).

The theory correctly reduces to known results as sanity checks: the equilibrium fixed point of the approximate (self-interaction-neglected) dynamics recovers the storage capacity from prior replica-method analyses (Gardner/Abbott's n-body Hopfield model), lending credibility to the derivation.

Interesting qualitative insight that, unlike the classical Hopfield model (n=2), for n≥3 the noise variance from non-recalled patterns does not grow with the overlap of the recalled pattern, offering a plausible explanation for improved robustness of higher-order/modern Hopfield architectures.

Numerical Monte Carlo evaluation of the theoretical overlap/attraction-basin predictions is compared against direct simulations (N=512, n=3) and shows reasonably good agreement, providing some empirical support for the theory.
The identification of the 'retarded self-interaction' term as the key qualitative difference from naive signal-to-noise analysis is a clear and interpretable structural finding.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is narrow: experiments are restricted to a single interaction order (n=3), a single system size (N=512), and a modest number of trials (100). No results are shown for larger n, different N, or comparisons of computation cost between GFA-based prediction and brute-force simulation.

The claimed contribution of 'quantitative characterization of convergence time' is not clearly delivered—the results shown are overlap trajectories and attraction-basin diagrams, but no explicit convergence-time metric (e.g., number of iterations to a threshold overlap as a function of α or n) is reported or analyzed in a dedicated figure/table.

The generality claim ('the methodology can be applied to other energy-based models' and to 'modern Hopfield networks, memory-augmented architectures') is asserted in the abstract, contributions, and conclusion but never demonstrated—the paper only treats the original polynomial-kernel dense associative memory and the classical n-body Hopfield model, not the Hopfield layer/continuous modern Hopfield networks that the introduction emphasizes as an important open problem.

Practical implications for 'model design' are stated repeatedly but never made concrete; it is unclear what actionable design guidance (e.g., choice of n, α, or T) the analysis yields beyond confirming known capacity results.

Writing quality has noticeable issues (grammatical errors, awkward phrasing such as 'before and after state transitions', 'It can be theoretically confirms', 'Preliminalies' typo in section heading), which detracts from readability and suggests limited proofreading.

The n=2 case, which is the most directly comparable and familiar baseline, is explicitly excluded from the main results and only referenced qualitatively, making it harder for readers to judge the magnitude of the claimed robustness improvement quantitatively.

The paper does not discuss computational complexity or scalability of solving the GFA saddle-point equations for large T, which is relevant to the claimed usefulness for practical model design and evaluation.

Limited comparison to alternative/simpler theoretical tools (e.g., mean-field/signal-to-noise approximations) beyond the single Corollary 1 special case, making it hard to assess how much added value the full GFA machinery provides beyond simpler heuristics in practical regimes.

strengths: The paper provides the first exact (asymptotic) dynamical treatment of Krotov-Hopfield dense associative memory using generating functional analysis (GFA), filling a genuine gap since prior work on this model only addressed equilibrium/storage-capacity properties via the replica method.

The derivation is carried out with reasonable rigor, and the appendices supply detailed proof sketches (combinatorial pairing arguments, saddle-point equations) that allow a knowledgeable reader to follow and, in principle, verify the calculations.

The theory is checked against Monte-Carlo simulations for n=3 (Figures 1 and 2), and the qualitative and quantitative agreement between predicted overlap trajectories/attraction basins and simulated ones is a useful sanity check.

The paper connects its dynamical result, in an approximate (non-retarded) limit, back to known equilibrium/replica results for the related n-body Hopfield model (Abbott & Arian), providing a consistency check with prior equilibrium theory.
weaknesses: The central 'no additional self-noise' claim advertised in the abstract is not fully supported by the paper's own results: Proposition 1 explicitly retains a 'retarded self-interaction' term (Γh)^(t) that couples the current state to its own past states in a complicated way; only the noise contributed by non-recalled patterns is shown to be overlap-independent. Conflating these two effects in the abstract/discussion risks overselling the robustness claim.

The analysis is restricted to the polynomial-kernel dense associative memory F(x)=x^n with n≥3 and binary patterns. The more practically influential and widely used 'modern Hopfield network' variant (the exponential/softmax Hopfield layer of Ramsauer et al. 2021, which underlies attention/Transformer connections) is explicitly excluded from the dynamical analysis, since the paper states it converges almost in one step; this substantially narrows the practical relevance of the results for an AI audience.

The claim of a 'general methodology for energy-based models' applicable beyond dense associative memory is asserted in the contributions list but only demonstrated for one closely related model (the n-body Hopfield model of Gardner/Abbott), which shares nearly identical combinatorial structure with the main model. No genuinely different energy-based architecture (e.g., continuous Hopfield layers, Boltzmann machines, energy transformers) is analyzed to substantiate generality.

Despite convergence time being highlighted as a key contribution in the abstract and introduction, no explicit quantitative formula, scaling law, or plot for convergence time is presented; the paper only qualitatively states convergence occurs 'within several tens of iterations.'

Numerical validation is limited to a single interaction order (n=3), one system size (N=512), and 100 trials; there is no exploration of how theory-simulation agreement changes with N, no results for larger n despite claims about 'large n' capacity, and finite-size effects near the basin boundary are acknowledged but not quantified.

The reported storage capacity value (α'_{c,3}=0.33) is not compared numerically against the original Krotov & Hopfield capacity claims or other independent estimates, leaving the practical significance of the number unverified.

The technical exposition is dense and contains inconsistencies/typos (e.g., mismatched notation ψ vs ϕ, duplicate definitions of Q^(t,t') and K^(t,t') in Eq. 15, 'PRELIMINALIES' section title, an apparent stray tilde-b term in Eq. 48) that reduce clarity and reproducibility for readers trying to verify the derivation independently.

The work is purely theoretical/statistical-mechanics in nature with no connection to any real machine learning task or empirical benchmark, which may limit its significance and audience within a broader AI venue relative to the effort required to parse the heavy formalism.

The novelty relative to the extensive prior GFA literature on Hopfield-type dynamics (Crisanti-Sompolinsky, Gardner et al., Coolen, etc.) is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (path probability, generating functional, saddle-point analysis) are directly inherited from decades-old methodology, with the main new content being the combinatorial extension to higher-order (n-body) interactions.
